note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: What share of seats in national parliaments are held by women?
questions.whyCorrect: 27.2% — just over a quarter, up from 22.3% in 2015. Women are half the world and hold roughly a quarter of the seats where laws are made.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — representation has improved substantially.
Nowhere near parity.
questions.action: Look up how many women are in your country's parliament.

questions.prompt: At the current pace, how long until women hold half of management jobs?
questions.whyCorrect: Nearly a century. Women's share of managerial roles rose only 2.4 percentage points in eight years, reaching about 30%.
whyWrong: Progress is roughly ten times slower than that.
Women hold under a third of management roles.
questions.action: Work out what year that would be. How old would you be?

questions.prompt: How much more unpaid work — cooking, cleaning, caring — do women do than men?
options: Two and a half times as much
questions.whyCorrect: Women spend two and a half times as many hours on unpaid domestic and care work. It's real work that no one pays for and no economy counts.
whyWrong: Women do substantially more, not less.
The gap is far larger than 'slightly'.
questions.action: Track who does what chores in your home for one week.

questions.prompt: How many young women were married before they turned 18?
questions.whyCorrect: 19% of women aged 20–24 were married as children. In sub-Saharan Africa it's 31% — nearly one in three.
whyWrong: Vastly too low.
Child marriage affects tens of millions of girls.
questions.action: Look up the legal marriage age where you live.

questions.prompt: How many girls and women alive today have undergone female genital mutilation?
questions.whyCorrect: Over 230 million, with about 4 million girls at risk each year — more than 2 million of them before age 5.
whyWrong: Vastly too low.
A hundred times too low.
questions.action: Find out which countries have banned the practice.

questions.prompt: Ending FGM by 2030 would need progress to speed up by how much?
questions.whyCorrect: 27 times faster than the current rate. On today's trajectory the practice will still be widespread well beyond 2030.
whyWrong: The gap between current and required pace is far larger.
It's one of the most badly off-track targets.
questions.action: Ask what makes a deeply rooted practice change.

questions.prompt: What share of married women can fully decide about their own reproductive health?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 56.3% — meaning nearly half of married women cannot freely make decisions about their own bodies and healthcare.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic, though the real figure is troubling.
Far too optimistic.
questions.action: Ask what 'full decision-making power' should include.

questions.prompt: In how many countries do fewer than half of women own or control farmland?
questions.whyCorrect: In nearly 80% of countries with data, fewer than half of women own or control agricultural land — even where women do most of the farming.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
Land ownership is heavily skewed against women almost everywhere.
questions.action: Ask why land ownership matters for independence.

questions.prompt: How many countries lack proper legal protection for women's land rights?
questions.whyCorrect: 58% of the 84 countries assessed lack adequate legal protections. Without law behind them, women's claims collapse in a dispute.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
The majority still lack adequate protections.
questions.action: Ask what a law needs to say to protect someone's property.

questions.prompt: Between 2019 and 2024, how many laws were changed to remove discrimination against women?
questions.whyCorrect: 99 positive legal reforms, mostly on employment rights and domestic violence protection. Genuine progress that rarely makes the news.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
There has been substantial legal reform.
questions.action: Look up one law in your country that changed for women's rights.

questions.prompt: Do women or men own more mobile phones?
questions.whyCorrect: 82% of men against 77% of women. A five-point gap sounds small, but across billions of people it's hundreds of millions of women without a phone — and phones mean banking, work and safety.
whyWrong: It runs the other way.
There's a measurable gap.
questions.action: Ask what you couldn't do without a phone.

questions.prompt: Which region has the highest share of women in management?
options: Australia/New Zealand and sub-Saharan Africa, over 40%
questions.whyCorrect: Over 40% in both Australia/New Zealand and sub-Saharan Africa — ahead of Europe and North America at about 39%. It surprises people that sub-Saharan Africa leads.
whyWrong: Several regions are above 39%.
This region fell to 11.6%, the lowest measured.
questions.action: Ask why sub-Saharan Africa might have high female management rates.

questions.prompt: In Central and Southern Asia, women's share of management roles recently:
questions.whyCorrect: It fell from 15.1% to 11.6% — one of the clearest examples of gender progress going backwards rather than forwards.
whyWrong: It declined rather than rose.
It's well below the global average of 30%.
questions.action: Ask what makes women's workplace gains reversible.

questions.prompt: Women's representation in LOCAL government is about:
questions.whyCorrect: 35.5% — higher than national parliaments at 27.2%, but it has stopped improving.
whyWrong: Local government has not reached parity.
It's substantially higher than 10%.
questions.action: Look up how many women are on your local council.

questions.prompt: Which region has the highest rate of child marriage?
questions.whyCorrect: Sub-Saharan Africa at 31% — nearly one in three young women married before 18, against a global figure of 19%.
whyWrong: Child marriage is rare in Europe.
Rates are very low in North America.
questions.action: Ask what makes families marry daughters young.

questions.prompt: Women's share of parliament seats rose how much since 2015?
questions.whyCorrect: Up 4.9 points, from 22.3% to 27.2%. Steady progress — but at this pace parity is generations away.
whyWrong: The gain was far smaller.
Representation rose rather than fell.
questions.action: Work out how long 23 more points takes at 0.5 a year.

questions.prompt: How many girls undergo FGM each year?
questions.whyCorrect: About 4 million girls a year — over 2 million of them before their fifth birthday.
whyWrong: A hundred times too low.
Vastly too low.
questions.action: Work out how many that is per day.

questions.prompt: Women hold what share of management positions worldwide?
questions.whyCorrect: About 30% — under a third, after rising just 2.4 percentage points in eight years.
whyWrong: Nowhere near parity.
Women are underrepresented, not overrepresented.
questions.action: Count the managers you know and their gender split.

questions.prompt: Legal reforms for women since 2019 focused mostly on:
questions.whyCorrect: The 99 reforms mostly targeted employment rights and protection from domestic violence — the two areas where discrimination in law was most common.
whyWrong: Not a focus of gender legal reform.
Voting ages generally apply equally already.
questions.action: Ask which of those two would change more lives.

questions.prompt: How does women's decision-making power over reproductive health vary between countries?
questions.whyCorrect: From 36.8% in some countries to 87.2% in others. Where a woman lives largely determines whether she controls her own healthcare.
whyWrong: The variation between countries is enormous.
Many countries are far below 90%.
questions.action: Ask what explains a 50-point gap between countries.

questions.prompt: If women do 2.5 times the unpaid work of men, what's the economic effect?
options: Less time available for paid work and study
questions.whyCorrect: Hours spent on unpaid care are hours not available for paid work, education or rest — which is a major reason women hold fewer senior roles.
whyWrong: It contributes to women earning less, not more.
Time is finite; unpaid work directly displaces paid work.
questions.action: Add up the hours of unpaid work done in your home weekly.

questions.prompt: The mobile phone gender parity score is 0.93. What does that mean?
options: Women own 93 phones for every 100 men own
questions.whyCorrect: A score of 0.93 means women's ownership is 93% of men's — 77% against 82%. A parity score of 1.0 would mean equality.
whyWrong: Equality would be a score of 1.0.
The score is below 1.0, meaning women own fewer.
questions.action: Ask what a phone gives access to that matters most.

questions.prompt: Which is closer to gender parity — national parliaments or local government?
questions.whyCorrect: Local government at 35.5% against national parliaments at 27.2%. Women are better represented closer to home — but local progress has stalled.
whyWrong: National parliaments lag behind local government.
There's an eight-point gap.
questions.action: Ask why it might be easier to be elected locally.

questions.prompt: In how many of 84 countries assessed are women's land rights adequately protected in law?
questions.whyCorrect: Only about 42% — since 58% lack adequate protections. Most countries still don't fully protect women's rights to land in law.
whyWrong: The majority lack adequate protections.
Far too optimistic.
questions.action: Ask what happens to a widow with no legal claim to her home.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of young women married as children is that, globally?
questions.whyCorrect: 19% — nearly one in five women aged 20–24 was married before turning 18.
whyWrong: Ten times too optimistic.
A hundred times too optimistic.
questions.action: Picture 20 young women. Roughly four were married as children.

questions.prompt: Europe and North America's share of women in management is about:
questions.whyCorrect: About 39% — slightly BELOW Australia/New Zealand and sub-Saharan Africa, both over 40%.
whyWrong: No region has reached this level.
That's closer to Central and Southern Asia's 11.6%.
questions.action: Ask whether you'd have guessed Europe led on this. It doesn't.

questions.prompt: How many girls undergo FGM before their fifth birthday each year?
questions.whyCorrect: Over 2 million of the 4 million girls affected annually are under five — too young to have any say at all.
whyWrong: It affects millions of very young girls.
A thousand times too low.
questions.action: Ask what protection a five-year-old can have in law.

questions.prompt: Women's management share rose 2.4 points in eight years. Is that fast?
options: No — it implies about a century to parity
questions.whyCorrect: At 0.3 points a year, closing a 20-point gap takes nearly 100 years. Slow progress and no progress feel very different but end up close.
whyWrong: Women hold about 30% of management roles.
The projection is roughly 70 years beyond 2030.
questions.action: Do the arithmetic yourself: 20 points at 0.3 a year.

questions.prompt: Which of these has gone BACKWARDS for women recently?
options: Management roles in Central and Southern Asia
questions.whyCorrect: Central and Southern Asia's female management share fell from 15.1% to 11.6%. Legal reforms and parliament seats both improved.
whyWrong: 99 discriminatory laws were removed between 2019 and 2024.
It rose 4.9 points since 2015.
questions.action: Ask what causes progress to reverse in one region but not others.

questions.prompt: Why does women's land ownership matter so much?
options: Land is collateral, security and inheritance
questions.whyCorrect: Land can be borrowed against, farmed with confidence and passed on. In nearly 80% of countries, fewer than half of women own or control farmland.
whyWrong: Land is often a family's single largest asset.
Households and farmers depend on land rights too.
questions.action: Ask who in your family's history owned land.

questions.prompt: Women hold 27.2% of parliament seats. What would parity look like?
questions.whyCorrect: Around 50%, since women are about half the population. At 27.2%, the world is roughly halfway there.
whyWrong: That's barely above the current figure.
That's the current figure, not the target.
questions.action: Work out how many more seats parity would mean in your parliament.

questions.prompt: Which everyday technology still shows a gender gap?
questions.whyCorrect: Mobile phone ownership: 82% of men against 77% of women. Phones now carry banking, work and emergency contact, so the gap has real consequences.
whyWrong: Not tracked as an SDG gender indicator.
Not tracked as an SDG gender indicator.
questions.action: List three things you do on a phone that matter for money or safety.

questions.prompt: Nearly 1 in 5 young women married before 18. What does early marriage usually mean for school?
questions.whyCorrect: Child marriage almost always ends a girl's education — which is why it is tracked alongside education and health outcomes rather than in isolation.
whyWrong: The effect on schooling is severe and well documented.
Married girls very rarely stay in school.
questions.action: Ask how ending school early changes someone's whole life.

questions.prompt: How many countries were assessed for women's land rights protections?
questions.whyCorrect: 84 countries, of which 58% lack adequate legal protection. Many countries have no data at all — itself part of the problem.
whyWrong: Ten times too few.
Not every country has data on this.
questions.action: Ask why missing data is its own kind of problem.

questions.prompt: Women's unpaid care work is described as 2.5 times men's. Is that work counted in the economy?
options: No — it's largely invisible in economic statistics
questions.whyCorrect: Unpaid care work is mostly absent from GDP and economic statistics, even though economies could not function without it.
whyWrong: Standard economic measures exclude most unpaid household work.
It's under-counted, not over-counted.
questions.action: Estimate what your household's unpaid work would cost to hire.

questions.prompt: Which is true about gender progress overall?
options: Real gains in law, very slow gains in power and money
questions.whyCorrect: 99 discriminatory laws were removed, but management parity is a century away and unpaid work is still 2.5 times higher for women. Legal change is outpacing lived change.
whyWrong: Management parity is projected to take about 100 years.
Parliament seats rose 4.9 points and 99 laws changed.
questions.action: Ask why changing a law is easier than changing a household.

questions.prompt: Sub-Saharan Africa leads on women in management but also leads on:
questions.whyCorrect: 31% of young women married before 18 — the highest rate of any region, even while it leads on women in management. Progress is rarely uniform.
whyWrong: Not the region's leading indicator.
Not the region's leading indicator.
questions.action: Ask how one region can lead on one measure and lag on another.

questions.prompt: Women's local government representation is stuck at 35.5%. What does 'stagnating' mean here?
questions.whyCorrect: It has plateaued — neither rising nor falling. Stalled progress is easy to miss because nothing dramatic happens.
whyWrong: Growth has stopped.
It's flat rather than declining.
questions.action: Ask what breaks a plateau.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many women and girls alive today have experienced FGM?
options: About the size of a small town
More than the population of most countries
questions.whyCorrect: Over 230 million — larger than the population of all but a handful of countries on Earth.
whyWrong: Vastly too low.
Vastly too low.
questions.action: Look up which countries have populations near 230 million.

questions.prompt: What share of women aged 15–49 in the surveyed countries lack full say over their own healthcare?
questions.whyCorrect: With 56.3% having full decision-making power, nearly 44% do not — close to half of married women in 78 countries surveyed.
whyWrong: Nearly half lack full decision-making power.
Far too optimistic.
questions.action: Ask who else might be making those decisions.

questions.prompt: Women are 50% of the world but hold what share of parliamentary seats?
questions.whyCorrect: 27.2% — roughly a quarter. Half the population, a quarter of the lawmaking power.
whyWrong: That would be parity, which hasn't been reached.
Women are underrepresented, not overrepresented.
questions.action: Compare 50% of people with 27% of seats.

questions.prompt: Which gender gap is smallest of these?
questions.whyCorrect: Phone ownership at 82% versus 77% is a 5-point gap — much narrower than management or parliament, though still hundreds of millions of women.
whyWrong: Women hold about 30% against parity of 50%.
Women hold 27.2% against parity of 50%.
questions.action: Rank those three gaps by how much you think they matter.

questions.prompt: The 99 legal reforms since 2019 show what?
options: Laws can change quickly when there's will
questions.whyCorrect: 99 discriminatory laws removed in five years shows legal change is achievable at pace — the harder part is changing what happens in homes and workplaces.
whyWrong: 99 reforms happened in five years.
Reforms occurred across many income levels.
questions.action: Ask what has to happen before a law actually changes lives.

questions.prompt: Child marriage globally affects 19% of young women. Ten years ago it was:
options: Higher — the rate is slowly falling
questions.whyCorrect: The rate has been declining slowly. Progress is real, but at this pace millions more girls will still be married as children before 2030.
whyWrong: The global rate has been falling, not rising.
There has been measurable decline.
questions.action: Ask what interventions reduce child marriage most.

questions.prompt: Why is women's representation in management tracked separately from parliament?
options: Economic power and political power are different things
questions.whyCorrect: A country can elect women to parliament while businesses stay male-led, or the reverse. Both matter, and they move at different speeds.
whyWrong: Management controls hiring, pay and promotion for millions.
Sub-Saharan Africa leads on management but not parliament, showing they diverge.
questions.action: Ask which kind of power changes daily life faster.

questions.prompt: What share of women own mobile phones?
questions.whyCorrect: 77%, against 82% of men. High overall, but the remaining gap represents hundreds of millions of women.
whyWrong: Too optimistic — nearly a quarter of women don't own one.
Too pessimistic — most women do own phones.
questions.action: Ask what someone without a phone can't access.

questions.prompt: Ending FGM needs 27x faster progress. What does that number tell you?
options: Current efforts are nowhere near sufficient
questions.whyCorrect: A 27-fold gap between current and required pace means the target will be missed by an enormous margin without a fundamental change in approach.
whyWrong: 4 million girls are still affected annually.
Rates have fallen in several countries, so change is possible.
questions.action: Ask what a 27x acceleration would actually require.

questions.prompt: Which statement about women's work is accurate?
options: They do most unpaid work and hold under a third of management jobs
They do less unpaid work and lead most companies
questions.whyCorrect: 2.5 times the unpaid work, and about 30% of management roles. The two facts are connected — unpaid hours crowd out career hours.
whyWrong: Both halves of this are the reverse of the data.
Neither paid nor unpaid work is split evenly.
questions.action: Ask how unpaid work at home shapes who gets promoted.

questions.prompt: Roughly what share of young women in sub-Saharan Africa were married before 18?
questions.whyCorrect: 31% — nearly one in three, well above the global rate of 19%.
whyWrong: Ten times too optimistic.
Too high, though the real figure is very high.
questions.action: Compare 31% regionally with 19% globally.

questions.prompt: What's the clearest sign gender equality is still far off?
options: Management parity is projected to take about 100 years
questions.whyCorrect: A century to reach equal management representation — that's students alive today spending their whole working lives before parity arrives.
whyWrong: This is genuine progress, not evidence of distance.
This is progress too, though slow.
questions.action: Work out what year parity arrives, and who'll be alive for it.
